idiom_name: duck-typed lock strategy injected in the constructor, used as `with self._lock:`
implementation_notes: The template parameter becomes a duck-typed constructor argument: any object implementing the lock protocol (acquire/release plus __enter__/__exit__) is a valid policy, and threading supplies Lock, RLock, Semaphore, BoundedSemaphore and Condition, with contextlib helpers for lock scoping. The with statement is Scoped Locking built into the language, so the guard class disappears and the remaining structure is the Thread-Safe Interface split - a public method takes the lock and calls a private _method that assumes it is held. Because the policy resolves at run time, a no-op strategy is a three-line stub; note that the GIL serializes bytecode rather than check-then-act sequences, so compound invariants still need a lock, and in free-threaded builds (3.13+, PEP 703) components that silently relied on the GIL need a real policy.
pitfalls: threading.Lock is not re-entrant - a method that takes the lock and calls another locking method deadlocks; RLock is the recursive policy, and choosing between them is the decision the strategy is supposed to make explicit.
Holding a lock across blocking I/O or long CPU work serializes unrelated callers and can hold it indefinitely; the GIL is released around I/O, which creates a false sense of safety.

threading locks are per-interpreter objects and cannot be shared with a child process (multiprocessing.Lock is the shared variant), and a daemon thread killed at interpreter shutdown can leave one held.
